section_1.title: Prerequisites: The 2D Area Foundation
section_1.content: Briefly review the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the 'signed area' of a parallelogram spanned by two vectors. Establish that a negative result indicates a change in orientation (right-hand vs. left-hand).
section_1.example: Visualize two vectors, a cat's paw reaching along the x-axis and y-axis; the area formed is the size of the square they bound.

section_2.title: Defining the 3D Cross Product
section_2.content: Transition to 3D space. The cross product of vectors u and v is defined as a vector perpendicular to both, with a magnitude equal to the area of the parallelogram formed by u and v. Introduce the Right-Hand Rule.
section_2.example: Imagine a robotic arm with two segments. The cross product represents the direction the joint needs to rotate to stay level with the surface formed by the two segments.

section_3.title: Linear Transformations and Volume
section_3.content: Explain the cross product as a linear transformation mechanism. If we transform 3D space, the cross product helps us understand how the 'orientation' and 'volume' of a 3D prism evolve.
section_3.example: Use a virtual cube in a game engine. As you scale or shear the cube, the cross product of its edges defines the surface normal, which is essential for calculating light reflection.

section_4.title: Visual Synthesis and Summary
section_4.content: Synthesize the concepts: The cross product is essentially a bridge between vector geometry and spatial orientation. It turns two lines into a direction that dictates how 3D objects 'face' the world.
section_4.example: Summary visual: A character pointing a flashlight. The direction of the beam (the 'Normal') is computed as the cross product of two vectors defining the light's tilt.
